w: Dr. Geisinger's starting point: if you treat every patient the same no matter their risk, you're set up to fail. Periodontitis isn't only an infection. It's an inflammation problem driven by the immune system, and how fast it moves (or whether it moves at all) depends on the patient, the specific site, and their environment. "One size does not fit all" is the theme. The practical question is: given what you know about this patient, how do you turn it into a recall schedule, a point where you step up treatment, and a conversation they'll act on? The scale of the problem, and who is actually looking About 42.5% of US adults over 30 have periodontitis (roughly 64.7 million people), rising to 70.1% of adults 65 and older. It's more common in men (56.4%) than women (38.4%), in current smokers (64.2%), in people below the poverty line (65.4%), and in people without a high school diploma (66.9%). The number that stings: 72% of patients who turn out to have periodontitis came in saying "I'm just here for my cleaning." Most have no idea. It doesn't hurt, bleeding when brushing feels normal, and nobody has measured or explained it to them. So the clinician is often the first and only person who will spot it. Billing data shows the gap. Dentistry bills procedures, not diagnoses. A "prophy" (code D1110) is a preventive cleaning meant only for people with no gum disease and no history of it. Since gum disease gets more common with age, prophy's share of cleanings should shrink as patients get older. Instead it grows: 72.3% of cleanings at ages 19-34, 87.5% at 35-49, and 95.4% at 50-64. That's the opposite of what should happen, which suggests disease is being missed (or not treated properly) more often as patients age. P4 (P5) medicine vs. Hippocratic medicine Traditional (Hippocratic) medicine starts from "do no harm," which in practice tends to mean reacting: treat disease once it shows up. P4 medicine means personalized, preventive, predictive and participatory: estimate each patient's risk, tailor it to their own risk factors, and make them an active partner in their care instead of someone who just gets instructions. For gum care the lecture adds a fifth P, periodontal, and calls it P5 care. Why is risk hard to estimate? Partly because "you get out what you put in." A bitewing that doesn't show the front teeth can hide the worst sites. A yearly panoramic-plus-bitewings routine may never picture the area that matters. In a UAB review of treated maintenance patients, over 40% of the records had to be thrown out because bleeding on probing had never been written down, and if you don't record inflammation, you can't tell how much the patient is carrying. A full risk workup, practically A risk workup has five parts: an interview (health history, lifestyle, whole-body conditions); a full gum exam (pocket depths, attachment levels, plaque, bleeding, pus, furcations, loose teeth, fremitus); X-rays to check bone levels; deciding whether you need the patient's physician (an HbA1c for a diabetic, an INR for someone on blood thinners); and a lifestyle check (tobacco, alcohol, stress). The American Academy of Periodontology recommends a full gum evaluation at least once a year for adults, more often for higher-risk patients, plus a quick screen at every visit. Why now? And what a 3 mm pocket means twice The hardest question patients ask, Dr. Geisinger says, is "why now?" Someone who never missed a six-month cleaning is suddenly told they have 8 mm pockets. Those pockets didn't appear overnight. The honest answer is usually a mix of not diagnosing, not treating, or "good enough" care that never reached below the gumline: repeated above-the-gum cleanings on someone who needed real gum treatment. The lecture's name for this is P.E.R.I.O.D. disease: Partially Effective, Redundant Instrumentation, Overlooking Disease. Cleaning only above the gums in a periodontitis patient improves plaque scores but doesn't shrink pockets or regain attachment. It actually raises bleeding and the number of 4 mm+ pockets, and shifts the bacteria under the gum toward nastier, oxygen-hating species (notably P. gingivalis). Something is not always better than nothing. It's also why a 3 mm pocket can mean two different things. After gum treatment, the gum reattaches with a long junctional epithelium, a thin skin-like seal, instead of the strong fiber attachment of healthy gums. That seal breaks down more easily when inflamed. So a treated patient with 3 mm everywhere still isn't a "prophy" patient the way someone who never had gum disease would be. They still need the periodontal maintenance code and schedule, because the tissue itself is built differently, even when the numbers look normal. The inflammatory burden, and why it isn't "just" a mouth problem The lecture makes this concrete with PISA (periodontal inflamed surface area): the total area of inflamed pocket lining. A healthy mouth averages about 34 mm², roughly a paper cut. Even mild-to-moderate (Stage 1-2) periodontitis averages about 2,309 mm², about the size of a wound from a spreading skin infection with early Ludwig's angina. That's why gum disease counts as an inflammation load on the whole body, not a local nuisance. It's linked to more than 50 body-wide conditions, and a few links have hard numbers: periodontitis raised the odds of dying after COVID-19 about nine-fold and of hospitalization about five-fold in one comparison; in a COPD trial, real below-the-gum treatment cut lung flare-ups about twice as much as above-the-gum cleaning or nothing; and in a diabetes trial, intensive gum treatment (full-mouth deep cleaning, surgery where needed, 3-month maintenance) brought HbA1c down from 8.1% to 7.8% over a year, while the above-the-gum-only group went from 8.1% up to 8.3% and had three deaths recorded as adverse events. Measuring risk with a tool instead of a gut feeling Scoring tools estimate risk better than gut feeling. UniFe (Trombelli) scores five things from 0 to 4: cigarettes per day, diabetes control (HbA1c), number of pockets 5 mm or deeper, percent of sites that bleed, and bone loss divided by age. The total puts the patient in one of five risk levels. The Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA) (Lang and Tonetti) and PreViser/PAT (Page) work the same way, combining exam, X-ray and lifestyle inputs into one risk level; UniFe and PreViser agreed fairly well when tested on the same patients. Newer AI tools (Pearl AI and Overjet were named) are joining them. None of them escape "garbage in, garbage out": they're only as good as the exam data you feed them. Turning a risk tier into an actual recall plan Once a patient is low, moderate or high risk, that level should change what you actually do: Low risk: full gum exam every 6-12 months, X-rays every 12-24 months, professional cleaning every 6 months, normal home care (brush twice a day, clean between teeth once a day), diet advice, and tobacco prevention. Moderate risk: full exam every 6-12 months plus a quick gum screen every 6 months, X-rays every 6-12 months, keep an eye on general health, cleaning plus spot deep-cleaning every 4-6 months, fix plaque traps, think about a local antimicrobial, surgery if needed to stop disease or repair defects, help quitting tobacco, extra hygiene tools (water or air flosser, rinses, probiotics), and check how well they keep up. High risk: full exam every 6-12 months plus a screen every 3 months, X-rays every 6 months, close health monitoring with physician consults, cleaning plus deep-cleaning every 2-4 months, think about systemic or local antibiotics, surgery likely, and the same home-care and quit-tobacco package, checked more closely. Why maintenance intervals are what they are Treated patients who skip maintenance lose teeth about twice as often as those who come back, and more frequent visits go with fewer teeth lost. Yet only about 30-40% of patients stick with maintenance. The 3-month interval isn't random: harmful bacteria start moving back under the gum 4-8 weeks after treatment, and by 9-11 weeks they can be back near where they started. A 3-month recall lands inside that window. Patients in active braces are seen even more often (about every 4-6 weeks), partly because that's when the braces get adjusted, and partly because inflammation while teeth are moving can throw off the balance of bone building and bone removal, risking real bone loss if plaque isn't tightly controlled. Coming regularly matters, not just the total number of visits, and it matters most for Stage 3-4 and Grade C patients: one who skips more than a year of maintenance over five years has about 2.5 times the odds of losing a tooth to gum disease. Communicating risk so patients actually act on it The number one reason patients say no to a gum treatment plan is that they don't trust their dental provider. The most trusted person in the office by far is the hygienist, not the dentist, which is why the whole team needs to give the same message. 62% of patients delay, switch dentists, get a second opinion, or refuse because they disagree with or doubt the diagnosis. Cost is rarely the real reason: patients say they'd pay about $633.63 per tooth to keep it. Cost becomes the objection when they feel rushed, can't ask questions, sense the team disagreeing, or aren't offered ways to manage the cost. In other words, when they don't yet feel you care about them. A stage-and-grade diagnosis ("Stage 2 Grade B periodontitis") gives everyone the same precise words. The lecture models moving a patient from cleanings to real treatment as a short conversation: say what you've been tracking and what it shows (the problem); explain plainly that once pockets are deeper than home care can reach, about 1.5-2 mm, bacteria settle in under the gum (the consequence); and lay out the "prescribed" (not just "proposed") plan and what it gains compared with doing nothing (the solution). The best predictors of a good long-term result are the same list this whole session covers: home hygiene, keeping up with maintenance, bleeding, pockets left after treatment, bite, bone loss for age, body-wide and genetic factors, and smoking. In class: the three prognosis systems, compared A prognosis is a prediction of how a tooth (or mouth) will do. The in-class Slido review, which Dr. Geisinger hinted "might inform the midterm," was about telling the three systems apart by what each one is asking, not by memorizing lists. McGuire & Nunn asks: can we keep this tooth? Most of the class guessed "will the disease get worse," which is wrong. Its order is good, fair, poor, questionable, hopeless, and the classic mistake is swapping poor and questionable. A "poor" tooth (lost attachment, Class II furcation, some looseness) can be kept, just with a lot of effort. A "questionable" tooth is one we honestly aren't sure we can keep, and it won't stay in that category: it either gets worse and becomes hopeless, or improves and moves up to poor. How accurate is it? Every statement in the poll was true. It's right about 80% of the time overall (81% at 8 years). Take out the teeth rated "good" and it drops to about 50%, a coin flip. On average teeth do better than predicted, and even "hopeless" teeth in well-maintained patients often last much longer than expected. The exceptions are smokers and people with very poor hygiene, and even very poor hygiene matches the prediction if those patients keep coming to maintenance. Most teeth leave the mouth because a dentist pulls them, not because they fall out on their own (unlike implants, which often do). McGuire & Nunn can be given for one tooth or the whole mouth, and as a diagnostic prognosis (what happens if the patient gets no treatment) or a therapeutic prognosis (how the recommended treatment changes things). The therapeutic version is a great way to show patients what treatment buys them. Kwok & Caton asks: can we stop the disease (get periodontal stability) with treatment? Answers run likely, don't know, unlikely. That's why "questionable" sits in the middle of its scale, and why it can only be therapeutic. It's the better pick for a medically complex patient, because quitting smoking or vaping and getting an A1c under control become part of the treatment it's judging. Miller & McEntire was studied only on molars. It uses numbers (A1c, smoking and other factors each get a score), and since it was built from patients who got 30 years of treatment and maintenance, it's therapeutic too. Smoking is its biggest single factor: about 296% more likely to lose those molars. The one-line summary: only McGuire & Nunn can be diagnostic; all three can be therapeutic. In class: three cases, all Stage 3 A 78-year-old (generally healthy with mild issues, on a statin and baby aspirin, #17 lost to a root-canal perforation) had mostly horizontal bone loss of about 30%, 5 mm or more of attachment loss between teeth at her worst site, and a Class II furcation. That's generalized Stage 3, Grade B, and her missing teeth were lost to cavities, not gum disease. First check the chart is right: was recession on the tongue side recorded? Her Kwok & Caton prognosis was questionable, because flat bone loss and furcations are hard to regrow. Plan: maintenance every 3 months (bacteria refill in about 9-11 weeks, and once someone has had periodontitis they stay higher-risk even when healthy), adjust her bite for trauma from chewing forces, and watch the recession. The PRA spider-web chart (bleeding, 5 mm+ sites, missing teeth, % bone loss, smoking) said to keep doing what she's doing. A 13-year-old with little plaque or inflammation had 8-11 mm pockets on her first molars and #14 in a molar-incisor pattern: localized Stage 3, Grade C. Deep, narrow vertical defects respond well to regrowing bone (bone graft, membrane, maybe a growth-factor product), filling about 70-75%, and young people heal better. So with treatment her McGuire & Nunn prognosis is good to fair overall, the affected teeth fair; without treatment it would be poor to questionable. Regrowing bone in the defect that set the stage is the only way to move someone back down from Stage 3. About 70% of kids with this around-puberty pattern have neutrophils (first-responder white blood cells) that don't move toward infection properly, which is why the first teeth to come in are hit hardest. About 70% of those whose disease later spreads use nicotine. She needs lifelong, more frequent maintenance and a strong anti-nicotine talk. A 75-year-old former smoker with bleeding at about 80% of sites, 7-9 mm pockets, and both vertical and flat bone loss is Stage 3, Grade C. Her overall McGuire & Nunn prognosis with no treatment is poor, even though individual teeth range from good to hopeless, which is why per-tooth prognoses are useful. With good cooperation plus bone reshaping or regrowing surgery, it improves to fair. If she later gets diabetes (A1c 8.8%), her grade can't go past C, but her PRA risk chart balloons. That's the point of keeping prognosis and risk tools separate from stage and grade: they catch differences the diagnosis can't. The closing numbers: about 10% of people resist periodontitis no matter their hygiene, 10-15% are at risk for severe disease, and 20-25% don't respond to standard treatment. Results depend on what patients control (hygiene, showing up for maintenance), exam findings (bleeding, leftover pockets, bite trauma, bone loss for age), and body-wide, genetic and nicotine factors.
